title: Scheduling & Autoscaling
summary: How the scheduler decides where a Pod runs, and how workloads and the cluster itself grow and shrink automatically.

slides.markdown:
**Requests** are what the scheduler reserves for a container — a node is only eligible if it has that much unallocated capacity. **Limits** are the hard ceiling the kubelet enforces at runtime: exceed the memory limit and the container is OOMKilled; exceed the CPU limit and it's throttled, not killed.

The scheduler only ever looks at **requests**, never limits, when deciding placement — a node can be scheduled well past its physical capacity if every Pod's limit is far above its request, which is exactly how overcommitment happens.

slides.subTitle: QoS classes
slides.markdown:
Kubernetes derives a **Quality of Service** class from how you set requests/limits, and uses it to decide eviction order under node pressure. **Guaranteed** (requests = limits, on every container) is evicted last. **Burstable** (requests set, limits higher or unset) is evicted before Guaranteed. **BestEffort** (no requests or limits at all) is evicted first.

Setting no requests doesn't make a Pod "free" — it makes it BestEffort, which is the first thing killed the moment a node runs short on memory.

slides.subTitle: Affinity and anti-affinity
slides.markdown:
**Node affinity** attracts Pods toward nodes with matching labels (e.g. `disktype=ssd`) — a preference or a hard requirement. **Pod affinity/anti-affinity** does the same relative to *other Pods*: co-locate a cache next to the service that uses it (affinity), or spread a Deployment's replicas across different nodes/zones so one node failure doesn't take all of them (anti-affinity).

Anti-affinity across zones is the standard way to make "3 replicas" actually mean 3 independent failure domains, not 3 Pods that happen to land on the same node.

slides.subTitle: Taints and tolerations
slides.markdown:
Affinity pulls Pods *toward* nodes; **taints** push Pods *away* by default.

| Mechanism | Direction | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Node affinity | Pod attracted to matching nodes | Pod prefers/requires certain nodes |
| Taint + toleration | Node repels Pods by default | Only Pods with a matching toleration may schedule there |

A taint like `dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule` blocks every Pod from that node except ones carrying a toleration for it — the standard way to reserve specialized nodes (GPU, spot) for only the workloads that opted in.

slides.subTitle: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
slides.markdown:
The **HPA** watches a metric (CPU %, memory, or a custom metric like queue depth) against a target you set, and adjusts a Deployment/StatefulSet's replica count to try to hit it — more replicas when the metric runs hot, fewer when it's idle, within min/max bounds you configure.

Scale-down is deliberately conservative (a stabilization window, default 5 minutes) to avoid flapping; scale-up reacts faster since under-capacity hurts users immediately while over-capacity just costs a little extra money.

slides.subTitle: VPA vs HPA
slides.markdown:
Two different axes of "more capacity."

| | HPA | VPA |
|---|---|---|
| Adds | More replicas (scale out) | More resources per replica (scale up) |
| Good for | Stateless, horizontally-scalable services | Workloads that can't be replicated, or right-sizing requests |
| Caveat | Needs a Service in front to load-balance | Currently requires a Pod restart to resize |

Running both against the same metric on the same workload can fight each other — a common production gotcha, since HPA wants more Pods while VPA wants bigger ones.

slides.subTitle: Cluster Autoscaler
slides.markdown:
HPA/VPA scale workloads within existing nodes; the **Cluster Autoscaler** scales the **nodes themselves**. It watches for Pods stuck **Pending** because no node has room, and adds a node from the configured pool; it also watches for underutilized nodes and removes them once their Pods can be safely rescheduled elsewhere.

This is the missing piece that makes HPA's "add more replicas" actually work when the current nodes are already full — without it, HPA can request Pods that simply never get scheduled.

slides.subTitle: A Pod stuck Pending
slides.markdown:
`kubectl describe pod` shows an event like "0/5 nodes are available: 5 Insufficient memory." That's a **scheduler** problem, not a bug — every node genuinely lacks the requested memory. Next check: is a Cluster Autoscaler configured and does it have room in its max-node bound to add capacity?

If events instead mention a taint with no matching toleration, or an anti-affinity rule with no valid node, that's a **placement constraint** problem, not a capacity one — adding nodes won't help until the constraint itself is fixed.

slides.subTitle: No resource requests set
slides.markdown:
**The wrong belief:** "skipping requests/limits means Pods just get what they need, no downside."

**Why it breaks:** a Pod with no requests is **BestEffort** QoS — first evicted under memory pressure — and the scheduler has no basis to reserve capacity, so it can land on an already-full node, causing unpredictable scheduling and noisy neighbors.

**The correct model:** set requests near real steady-state usage (from metrics, not guesses), and limits deliberately — loose enough for bursts, tight enough to protect neighbors.
